would_stay_after_2s: yes. The first line compares it to my own kitchen knife that rusts if I leave it wet, then says this sword is still bright after 2000+ years. That is a concrete contradiction and I want to know how. Also, 'bright' is highlighted, so my eye lands on it.
swipe_moments: 14.75-23.25 (lines 4-5): museum, Japan, Singapore, export ban since 2013. This is trivia with no answer to the hook yet. If it drags I would swipe here. The 'chrome-plated' rumor at 18.75 saves it a little because it sets up a myth I expect to see debunked.
23.25-40.75 (tomb dig, 10.8m, rammed earth, two coffins): about 17s of scene-setting. It is a bit long, though 'never been robbed' and 'sword in black lacquer sheath' keep a thin thread of story.
48.75-58.25 (the 鸠浅 / 勾践 reading, 40 letters): this is the real lull. It's a side story about reading the inscription, not about rust. I'd start to wonder if the video forgot the question.
70.5-74.0 (tin 18%-20%, lead near zero): numbers with no explanation of why they matter. A quick swipe risk.
confusing_lines: Line 5 (18.75): 'chrome-plated, so it doesn't rust' is shown as a popular claim but is never clearly marked right or wrong. I had to wait until the end to guess it was false. Chromium is never named again.
Line 17 (70.5): '含锡约18%-20%，铅几乎为零，料很纯' - why does tin or lead matter? Never connected to rust.
Line 18 (74.0): '菱形花纹是热镀锡做的' - 7 years of research, then dropped. Does the tin coating protect it or not? Unclear. It also seems to quietly answer the chrome claim, but isn't stated.
Line 3 (14.75) vs 23.25 jump: 'it's in Hubei museum' then suddenly '1965 winter' - fine, but 'Chu tomb' vs 'Yue king' only gets explained at 58.25.
Line 12 (61.25): 'why is a Yue king's sword in a Chu tomb' is raised and then left with 'no conclusion'. Feels like an open loop, mildly unsatisfying.
best_line: 「它不是不会锈，是那座墓，替它挡了两千多年。」(107.25) - a clean reversal of the opening, and I could repeat it to a friend. Runner-up: 「其实，它也锈了。」(82.0) - the pause before it and the short line make it the real turn.
what_you_remember: The Goujian sword isn't rust-proof or secretly chrome-plated; it rusted a little too, and the sealed tomb is what kept it looking new.
would_you_comment_or_share: Maybe comment, share only to a history-nerd friend or a dorm group chat that argues about 'ancient tech'. I would comment something like '我一直以为是镀铬的，被骗了这么多年' because the myth debunk is what stuck. I'd tag a friend who told me the chrome story. The ending question 'where did you first see it?' invites a reply too (for me: 历史课本 / 湖北博物馆).
title_pick: 「越王勾践剑，真的没锈吗？」 - it asks the exact question the video overturns, and 'really?' signals a myth-bust, which I click on. 「越王勾践剑 / 为什么不锈？」 is okay but assumes the sword doesn't rust, which the video says is false, so it slightly misleads. 「埋两千多年，为何还亮？」 is the most intriguing curiosity hook, but it also repeats the false premise that it is still bright (the video says it got less bright after excavation).
title_that_misleads: 「越王勾践剑 / 为什么不锈？」 - the answer is 'it did rust, just lightly'. 「埋两千多年，为何还亮？」 is slightly misleading too, since the video says it dulled after excavation.
